newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian chancellor vows to stay, criticism grows.
newsitem.headline: Austrian chancellor vows to stay, criticism grows.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, squaring up to his critics for the first time since his party's poor performance in European Parliament elections, said on Saturday he had no intention of resigning.

Vranitzky, whose Social Democrats slumped to a post-1918 low in Sunday's poll, said he was determined to stay on as chancellor and party leader and he took issue with dissenting voices within Social Democrat ranks.

"It is neither fair nor productive to attack me," Vranitzky, chancellor since 1986, told Austrian radio. "I am ready to give my all to continue my work and I do not consider our chances of success have diminished as a result of Sunday," he added.

But the former banker's fighting talk did little to quell a raging debate about his suitability as leader. Social Democrats and normally sympathetic union bosses have cast doubt on Vranitzky's ability to turn party fortunes around.
Party vice-leader Franz Loeschnak, the most senior Social Democrat to date, on Saturday added his voice to calls for sweeping changes at the top.
"We can no longer repress a discussion about the party line-up," Loeschnak told Die Presse newspaper.

And Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl, whose absolute majority has disappeared in the city known for decades as "Red Vienna", poured fuel on the flames when he said the chancellor should not step down "yet". "The position of chancellor is not written in stone," Haeupl said.
An unbowed Vranitzky, in office since 1986 and Europe's longest serving head of government after Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany, gave a spirited defence of his political record.
"There will be no change of course. The economy is in good shape. Inflation and unemployment are among the lowest in Europe and investments and exports are booming," he said.

But the chancellor, 59, conceded that the Social Democrats had not succeeded in awakening a "feel-good factor" among Austrian voters. "We have to get away from the raw data and speak to emotions. We failed to do that on October 13."
More than 50 percent of working class voters, the traditional backbone of Social Democrat support, backed the far-right Freedom Party of Joerg Haider last Sunday.

With only 29.1 percent of the ballot, the Social Democrats fell behind coalition partner the People's Party for the first time in 30 years and finished just 60,000 votes ahead of Haider's nationalist movement.
"We have to stand by our belief in solidarity and loyalty and challenge (Haider's) arguments that arouse social envy and the conviction that everything foreign is bad," Vranitzky said.
Haider's anti-immigrant invective has struck a chord with ordinary Austrians fearful of losing their jobs and access to public housing.
Vranitzky refused to join media speculation about his successor. Austrian political commentators and some Social Democrats rate Finance Minister Viktor Klima heir apparent.
Klima offered the chancellor his backing on Friday but stopped short of saying he had no ambitions for his job.
